newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ dollar bought, then sold after coalition deal.
newsitem.headline: NZ dollar bought, then sold after coalition deal.

text.p: The New Zealand dollar was sharply bid up on Tuesday night after New Zealand First announced a coalition deal with the National Party, before being sold down just as suddenly.
Dealers said the Kiwi went to a high of US$0.7100 before sinking almost a cent back to US$0.7015 by 11.00 p.m. (1000 GMT). Kiwi was trading around 0.7050 just before the announcement.

"We view it as positive for both short and long-term interest rates. We think the currency may weaken over time due to Mr Peters' stated desire for a lower Kiwi and the strong likelihood for a monetary policy easing next week," he said.

The key platforms of National's economic policy -- inflation control, decentralised wage bargaining and commitment to fiscal responsibility -- remained broadly intact after weeks of coalition negotiations.
Chris Rand, Chief Manager of Foreign Exchange and Money Markets at Westpac, said the currency had run into selling at 0.7100.

"Everyone is sort of talking: is Winston Peters a good guy for Treasurer; do we want him as deputy PM; should we be getting out of the market; and what the Reserve Bank is going to do next Tuesday," said one Auckland dealer.
"It's opened the door for an easing now."
"To me it all looks bearish from here and you've got a Treasurer who is re-endorsing a lower Kiwi anyway," he said
The Reserve Bank releases its Monetary Policy Statement on Tuesday.
Bankers Trust Economist David Plank assessed the deal as favourable for financial markets.

"What's happened since then is people have taken notice of the fact that one of things he said at the start of the speech was that he's got agreement for policies which he believes will correct the problem of the over-valued dollar," he said.
"Also the inflation target has been widened and it's got a higher mid-point than it used to have at one and a half (percent), so people are anticipating lower rates.
"There's potential for rates to go lower in this particular easing cycle than I think the market had previously anticipated," Rand said.
Westpac economists reckoned short-term rates could drop to the high seven percents, but the futures market had gone further and was showing rates closer to seven percent by March.
The unspecified growth target attached to the RB policy agreement was another disincentive for people to go long.
Rand said Don Brash staying on as Reserve Bank governor was a stabilising factor.
"But what people are focusing on is that Peters did quite clearly say there was agreement on policies that would correct the problem of the overvalued dollar.

"I expect that the market will sit and wait now till tomorrow morning to see what comes out with these further policy announcements...exactly what the growth target is going to be and how it's going to be monitored..."
From here, the currency could be expected to find support at 0.6980 with resistance at 0.7050.
